title: Impact of Police Staffing on Crime Rates

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Causal method: Two-Stage Least Squares (Instrumental Variables).

Why IV? Police staffing (x) is likely endogenous: jurisdictions often hire more officers in reaction to rising crime, creating reverse causality and omitted-variable bias.  
The cops-grant lottery (z) randomly allocates additional funding for officers, supplying exogenous variation in police staffing that is unrelated to contemporaneous crime levels except through staffing.

Key assumptions  
1. Relevance: z is correlated with police staffing (Cov(z, x) ≠ 0).  
2. Exclusion Restriction: z affects crime rates (y) only through its impact on staffing, not through any other channel.  
3. Independence/Random Assignment: conditional on controls, z is as-good-as randomly assigned.

Under these assumptions, 2SLS identifies the causal effect of police staffing on crime.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(AER)        # for ivreg
library(sandwich)   # robust vcov
library(lmtest)     # coeftest
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Read data -------------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s84_data.csv",
               col_types = cols(
                 y        = col_double(),
                 x        = col_double(),
                 z        = col_integer(),
                 controls = col_double()
               ))

# 2. OLS benchmark ---------------------------------------------------------
ols_mod <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
ols_robust <- coeftest(ols_mod, vcov = vcovHC(ols_mod, type = "HC1"))

# 3. IV (2SLS) -------------------------------------------------------------
iv_mod <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)
iv_robust <- coeftest(iv_mod, vcov = vcovHC(iv_mod, type = "HC1"))

# 4. First-stage diagnostics ----------------------------------------------
first_stage <- iv_mod$stage1
fs_robust   <- coeftest(first_stage, vcov = vcovHC(first_stage, type = "HC1"))
fs_fstat    <- linearHypothesis(first_stage, "z = 0", vcov = vcovHC(first_stage, type="HC1"))$"F"[2]

# 5. Weak-instrument rule-of-thumb ----------------------------------------
cat("First-stage F-statistic on z (robust):", round(fs_fstat,2), "\n\n")

# 6. Print main results ----------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(
  list("OLS" = ols_mod, "2SLS" = iv_mod),
  vcov = list(vcovHC(ols_mod, type="HC1"), vcovHC(iv_mod, type="HC1")),
  statistic = "({stat})",
  stars = TRUE
)

# 7. Sensitivity: drop controls -------------------------------------------
iv_nocontrol <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = df)
iv_nocontrol_robust <- coeftest(iv_nocontrol, vcov = vcovHC(iv_nocontrol, type = "HC1"))

cat("\nRobust IV estimate without controls:\n")
print(iv_nocontrol_robust["x",])

# 8. End
```

The script:
• Reads the CSV at the specified path.  
• Shows an OLS estimate for comparison.  
• Implements 2SLS with `z` as the instrument, reports robust (HC1) standard errors, and prints the first-stage F-statistic to assess instrument strength.  
• Provides a robustness check by re-estimating the IV model without the socioeconomic controls.

## 3. Expected Findings
Sign: Negative. More police officers should lower crime.  

Magnitude: With standardized variables (mean ≈ 0, sd ≈ 1), a one-standard-deviation increase in police staffing is expected to cut crime by roughly 0.3–0.5 standard deviations. Thus the 2SLS coefficient on x should be around –0.30 to –0.50, larger in magnitude than the biased OLS estimate.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use the cops grant lottery as an instrument for police count.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Increased police staffing significantly reduces crime rates.
